sentences.text: This notebook automates the cash application process by matching incoming bank receipts to open accounts receivable invoices.
It produces three key outputs: allocation lines detailing how each receipt is applied, updated statuses for open items, and a snapshot of the accounts receivable aging.

The process is controlled by parameters for the source data location, the run date, and the specific company code, with a default setting that prevents changes from being saved unless explicitly enabled.
When run in its default mode, the notebook processes the data and displays summaries without permanently updating the target tables.

sentences.text: The process reads five source files from a designated raw data folder.
These files contain bank receipts, open invoice items, customer details, manual accounting overrides, and foreign exchange rates.
The run is controlled by parameters for the company, the processing date, and whether to save the results.
The primary output is a detailed record of how each payment was applied to invoices.
This record is saved to the fin_cash.alloc_lines table, replacing the previous version of the data.
The process also updates the list of outstanding invoices in the fin_cash.open_items_after table.
A snapshot of the accounts receivable aging is added to the fin_cash.ar_aging_snap table.
Stakeholders receive an HTML summary report detailing suspense accounts, unapplied payments, and write-offs.
A log entry is created to record the run's performance and key counts.
The engine processes bank receipts to match them against open invoices, using a strict priority system to identify the correct customer for each payment.
It then allocates the receipt amount to specific invoices through a sequence of matching methods, finally updating the status of the invoices and generating an aging report.
First, the system filters incoming bank receipts to include only those with a positive amount and a value date on or before the run date.
Receipts are mapped to specific company codes using a predefined list of bank accounts, and any receipt from an unrecognized account is silently dropped.
The system identifies the customer for each receipt by prioritizing manual overrides, then document references found in the remittance text, and finally normalized customer name matching.
Open invoices are filtered to include only those with a positive balance, and specific customers are excluded from the matching pool entirely.
All amounts are converted to USD using the most recent exchange rate for the respective currency, ignoring the specific date of the transaction.
Allocation begins by matching the receipt to specific document numbers listed in the remittance text, skipping any documents that are not in the open pool or have a zero balance.

If no document references are found, the system looks for an open invoice whose remaining balance exactly matches the receipt amount within a tolerance of 0.01, selecting the oldest invoice if multiple match.
If the receipt amount still exceeds a threshold of 5.0, the remaining balance is allocated to open invoices in the same pool, sorted by largest balance first, skipping any disputed items.
Any invoice touched by the allocation that has a remaining balance of 5.0 or less is written off and zeroed out.
If a portion of the receipt remains unallocated after these steps, it is marked as 'UNAPP' if a customer was identified, or 'SUSP' if no customer could be determined.

Finally, the system updates the status of all open invoices to 'CLEARED', 'PARTIAL', or 'OPEN' based on their remaining balance, and generates an aging snapshot for items with a balance greater than 0.005.
Small leftover amounts on invoices are silently written off up to 5.00 USD instead of the intended 0.50 USD, meaning minor discrepancies are absorbed without being flagged for review.
If a receipt is in a currency not present in the exchange rate table, its converted value becomes null, which can cause the entire receipt to be unapplied or misreported.

Receipts are converted to USD using the most recent exchange rate rather than the rate on the receipt's value date, which can cause the reported amounts to differ from the actual value on the day the money was received.
The allocation step named 'FIFO' actually allocates to the largest open invoices first rather than the oldest, which may contradict the business expectation that older debts are cleared first.

Receipts are processed in a specific order, and because the allocation logic modifies the remaining balances of invoices as it goes, the order in which receipts are processed determines which invoices get paid, potentially leading to different results if the order changes.

If the notebook is run in dry-run mode, stakeholders still receive notifications and run logs as if the data was saved, even though no actual data is written to the tables, which can cause confusion about whether the data is up to date.
When the notebook is run for real, the allocation lines and updated open items tables are overwritten, meaning a failed or partial run can wipe out previously correct data.
The AR aging snapshot table is appended to rather than overwritten, so re-running the notebook for the same date will create duplicate rows unless downstream processes deduplicate them.
Receipts that do not match a bank account in the hardcoded mapping are silently dropped from the dataset, meaning some incoming money may never be processed.

The general ledger account mapping is imported from an external notebook, so if that external notebook changes its logic, the GL assignments in this process will change without any local code modification.
A safeguard intended to cap write-off amounts at 250.00 USD was defined but never used, meaning there is no limit on how much can be written off in a single step.
If a document reference in a receipt points to an invoice in a different company or pool, it will still be allocated, which may result in cross-company allocations that are not intended.
Negative balances on open items are only warned about and not stopped, so over-allocations can still be written to the output tables.
The reconciliation check that compares allocated amounts to original receipt amounts only prints the first 20 mismatches and does not stop the run, so significant errors may go unnoticed.
The company-level reconciliation only triggers a warning if the difference exceeds 0.01 USD, but the run does not stop, so small but persistent breaks may accumulate.

Inquire about the impact of processing receipts sequentially, as the order determines which open invoices are allocated to which receipts.

Confirm whether stakeholders should receive notifications during dry runs, as the system logs and alerts even when no data is persisted.
Ask if the overwrite mode for allocation lines is acceptable, given that a partial failure can wipe previously correct data.

The pipeline begins by reading five CSV files from a configurable source directory: bank_receipts.csv, open_items.csv, customers.csv, ar_overrides.csv, and fx_rates.csv.
These files are loaded into Spark DataFrames, which are then enriched with derived columns such as customer pool assignments and normalized reference data.

The enriched Spark DataFrames are converted to Pandas DataFrames to facilitate Python-based allocation logic, where receipts are matched to open items using override, reference, or name-based methods.

The resulting allocation lines are enriched with currency and metadata information, validated, and finally written to three Delta tables: fin_cash.alloc_lines, fin_cash.open_items_after, and fin_cash.ar_aging_snap.
r: The primary receipt DataFrame, built from bank_receipts.csv and enriched with run date, metadata, and matching results.
oi: The open items DataFrame, built from open_items.csv and filtered by exclusion rules and customer data.
cm: The customers DataFrame, built from customers.csv, containing the derived 'pool' column which uses the parent number if available, otherwise the customer number.
ov: The AR overrides DataFrame, built from ar_overrides.csv, used for high-priority receipt matching.
fx: The FX rates DataFrame, built from fx_rates.csv, used to convert amounts to USD.
rr: The enriched receipt DataFrame, combining receipt data with override, reference, and name match results, and updated with FX rates and customer data.
rp: A Pandas DataFrame containing receipt details, converted from the Spark DataFrame rr for allocation logic.
ip: A Pandas DataFrame containing open item details, converted from the Spark DataFrame oi2 for allocation logic.
bal, meta, pools: Python dictionaries built from the open items Pandas DataFrame, mapping document numbers to balances, metadata, and pool assignments respectively.
ln: The allocation lines DataFrame, built from the allocation logic and enriched with receipt and open item metadata, including currency, rates, and customer information.
fin_cash.alloc_lines: The final output table containing 13 columns of allocation details, written in Delta format when not in dry-run mode.
fin_cash.open_items_after: The output table containing the state of open items after allocation, written in Delta format when not in dry-run mode.
fin_cash.ar_aging_snap: The output table containing an aging snapshot of accounts receivable, written in Delta format in append mode when not in dry-run mode.
The engine applies a strict sequence of filters, matching logic, and calculations to allocate receipts to open items.
The process begins by filtering receipts to include only those with a positive amount and a value date on or before the run date.
Receipts that do not match a bank account in the hardcoded mapping are silently dropped from the dataset.
Bank account identifiers are mapped to company codes using a hardcoded dictionary, where 'DB-4471' maps to 'DK01' and 'JPM-2290' maps to 'US01'.
Open items are filtered to include only those with a positive open amount, excluding fully paid or credit items.
Open items for customers 'C10077' and 'C10412' are excluded from the matching pool via the EXCL list, meaning receipts from these customers can never be matched to their invoices.
The 'dispute' column in open items is converted from a string 'Y' to a numeric 1, with all other values becoming 0.
Customer aliases are normalized by uppercasing, removing non-alphanumeric characters, and stripping legal suffixes like 'LTD' and 'GMBH' to improve name matching.
Document numbers are extracted from remittance text using a regex that finds 8-digit numbers starting with 9, ensuring they are not part of a longer number.
Customer identification for a receipt prioritizes manual overrides (c_ov) over document reference matches (c_ref), which in turn take priority over name matches (c_nm).
The USD conversion rate for receipts is determined by taking the most recent FX rate for the currency, ignoring the specific value date of the receipt.
Open items are converted to USD using the latest FX rate for their document currency, stored in the 'open_usd' column.

Allocation proceeds in four sequential steps per receipt: first, exact document reference matching (REF); second, exact amount matching within a tolerance (EXACT); third, FIFO-style allocation by largest balance (FIFO); and finally, write-off of small residual balances (WO).
In the main allocation loop, receipts are processed in order of val_dt then rcpt_id.

The apply_ref function allocates a receipt amount to specific document numbers listed in the receipt's refs field, in the order they appear, skipping documents not in bal or with zero balance, and records each allocation as a 'REF' line.
The apply_exact function is attempted only if no REF lines were produced and the receipt has a customer.

The apply_exact function finds open items in the same pool whose remaining balance exactly matches the receipt amount within a tolerance of 0.01, picks the one with the earliest doc_dt, and records the allocation as an 'EXACT' line.
The apply_fifo function is attempted only if the remainder exceeds TOL and the receipt has a customer.
The FIFO allocation step does not sort by due date as the name implies; instead, it sorts open items by descending balance (largest first) and allocates against them in that order.

The apply_fifo function allocates the remaining receipt amount across open items in the same pool, skipping disputed items, and records each partial allocation as a 'FIFO' line; it stops when the remainder drops to 0.005 or below.

The do_wo function writes off any document that was touched by this receipt (via REF, EXACT, or FIFO) if its remaining balance is positive but at or below TOL, recording a 'WO' line and zeroing the balance.
The tolerance variable TOL is initially set to 0.5 but is later reassigned to 5.0; the constant EX_TOL is set to 0.01 for exact amount matching.
After all allocation attempts, any remaining amount above 0.005 is recorded as 'UNAPP' if the receipt has a customer, or 'SUSP' if it does not, indicating unapplied or suspicious receipts.

The receipt-currency amount (amt_rc) is derived by dividing the USD amount by the receipt's exchange rate (r_rate), and the document-currency amount (amt_dc) is derived by dividing the USD amount by the document's exchange rate (i_rate); both are rounded to 2 decimal places.

For each receipt, the sum of all non-write-off allocation lines (REF, EXACT, FIFO) in receipt currency must equal the original receipt amount; any discrepancy is added to the last non-WO line for that receipt, and if the document currency matches the receipt currency, the same adjustment is applied to the document-currency amount.

The GL account for each allocation line is determined by the company code and the line type: types REF, EXACT, and FIFO all map to the 'AR' key in the company's GL map, while other types (WO, UNAPP, SUSP) use their own type name as the key.

Open items whose remaining USD balance is less than 0.005 are set to zero and marked 'CLEARED'; those with a remaining amount less than the original open amount are marked 'PARTIAL'; all others remain 'OPEN'.
The AR aging snapshot includes only open items with a remaining USD balance greater than 0.005, so fully cleared or near-zero items are excluded from the aging report.
Key accounts (customers with grp='KEY') that have unapplied cash exceeding 10,000 USD are flagged in the AR notification email as a special alert.
The notebook writes to three Delta tables only when the dry-run flag is set to 'N'.
The allocation lines are written to fin_cash.alloc_lines in overwrite mode with the overwriteSchema option enabled.
The updated open-items balances are written to fin_cash.open_items_after in overwrite mode.
The AR aging snapshot is appended to fin_cash.ar_aging_snap rather than overwritten.
The fin_cash.alloc_lines table has a fixed schema of 13 columns plus a load timestamp column added at write time.
In dry-run mode, the three output tables are not written, but external functions are still called.
Stakeholders receive notifications and run logs even when no data is persisted during a dry run.
An HTML-formatted summary containing counts and USD totals for suspense, unapplied, and write-off lines is sent via the notify_ar function.

The run is logged via log_run with the notebook name 'cash_app_v3', the run date, and a dictionary containing receipt count, line count, suspense count, write-off count, elapsed seconds, and the dry-run flag.
The notebook depends on the external file ../shared/fin_utils, which is loaded inline using %run.
This shared notebook provides functions such as log_run, notify_ar, and get_gl_map that are used later in the process.
The get_gl_map function is called once per unique company code present in the allocation lines.
The notebook unconditionally sets the Spark configuration spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 8.
This configuration change affects the execution of all subsequent Spark operations in the session, not just this notebook's queries.
The notebook relies on Databricks runtime globals including dbutils, spark, and display.
The variable TOL is initially set to 0.5 USD but is reassigned to 5.0 USD later in the notebook, so the write-off step silently absorbs residuals up to 5.00 USD instead of flagging them.
The constant MAX_WO is defined as 250.0 but is never used, suggesting a missing safeguard that was intended to cap write-off amounts.
The function named apply_fifo sorts open items by descending balance (largest first) rather than by date, which contradicts the typical first-in-first-out expectation implied by the name.
The global dictionary bal is mutated in place by all allocation functions, so the sequential order of processing receipts affects which open items are available for subsequent allocations.

The FX rate used for converting receipt amounts to USD is the latest available rate for the currency, not the rate on the receipt's value date, which can cause mismatches for small-value items in high-value currencies.
If a receipt's currency is not present in the FX rates table, the exchange rate will be null, resulting in a null USD amount for that receipt.
Receipts that do not match a bank account in the hardcoded mapping are silently dropped from the dataset without any warning.

The apply_ref function does not check whether a referenced document belongs to the same pool or company as the receipt, so cross-pool references may be allocated if the document exists in the balance dictionary.

The write-off step only considers documents that were touched by the current receipt's allocation, so a document reduced to a small residual by a previous receipt will not be written off until a subsequent receipt touches it.

The function alloc_by_aging is defined but never called; it implements a more sophisticated aging-based allocation that skips disputed invoices, while the actual FIFO step uses a simpler largest-balance-first approach.

The GL account mapping is determined by an external function imported from another notebook, so changes to that external logic will affect this notebook's GL assignments without any local code modification.
In dry-run mode, the output tables are not written, but external functions for notifications and run logging are still called, meaning stakeholders receive updates even when no data is persisted.
The aging snapshot table is written in append mode, so re-running the notebook for the same date will create duplicate rows unless downstream processes deduplicate by run date.
When the dry-run flag is disabled, the allocation lines table is written in overwrite mode with schema overwrite enabled, meaning a failed or partial run can wipe previously correct data.

Reconciliation checks that detect mismatches between allocated amounts and original receipt amounts only print the first 20 offenders and do not stop the run, so the notebook can complete successfully even with unresolved discrepancies.
Several imports and code blocks are dead code, including unused imports of math and reduce, and commented-out cells containing old matching logic and fuzzy matching routines.

sections.title: How to check that a change is safe

sentences.text: Use the dry-run flag to isolate logic changes from side effects.
Set the 'dry' widget to 'Y' to prevent writes to fin_cash.alloc_lines, fin_cash.open_items_after, and fin_cash.ar_aging_snap.
Note that even in dry-run mode, the external functions notify_ar and log_run are still called, so stakeholders may receive alerts.
Verify that the sum of non-write-off allocation lines (REF, EXACT, FIFO) for each receipt equals the original receipt amount in receipt currency.
Check the reconciliation output for 'CO RECON BREAK' warnings, which indicate a company-level difference exceeding 0.01 USD between bank receipts and allocated lines.
Inspect the 'bad' variable count from the reconciliation check in cell C34 to identify receipts with mismatches, noting that the run does not stop on failure.
Confirm that no open items have negative balances below -0.005 USD by checking the output of the check_bal function.
Be aware that check_bal only prints a warning and returns a count; it does not raise an exception, so negative balances may still be written to output tables.
Verify that open items with a remaining balance less than 0.005 USD are correctly set to zero in the open_items_after table.
When changing allocation logic, verify that the TOL variable is 5.0 USD in the write-off step, as it is reassigned from 0.5 to 5.0 in cell C29.
Ensure that residuals up to 5.00 USD are intentionally written off by the do_wo function rather than flagged as unapplied.
Check that the FIFO allocation step sorts open items by descending balance, not by due date, to confirm the intended allocation order.
Validate that customer identification follows the priority: manual overrides, then document references, then name matches.
Confirm that receipts with a null 'id_src' are correctly identified as unlinked to a source system in cell C27.
Review the top 10 pools by total USD amount for receipts with a non-null customer to sanity-check the customer-to-pool mapping.
If writing to production (dry='N'), verify that fin_cash.ar_aging_snap is appended to, not overwritten, to avoid duplicate rows on re-runs.
Check that fin_cash.alloc_lines and fin_cash.open_items_after are written in overwrite mode, which can wipe previous data if the run fails partially.
Ensure that the 'run_dt' parameter is set correctly, as it determines the cutoff for receipt inclusion and defaults to the current system date if empty.
Verify that receipts are filtered to include only those with a positive amount and a value date on or before the run date.
Check that receipts not matching a bank account in the hardcoded mapping are silently dropped, and confirm this is the intended behavior.
Ensure that the FX rate used for USD conversion is the latest available rate for the currency, not the rate on the receipt's value date.
Identify receipts with a null 'r_rate' (and thus null 'amt_usd') to detect currencies missing from the FX rates table.
